options: Finding a value at the intersection of a row condition and a column condition, like Region = West and Month = March
Looking up the same value in two different workbooks
A lookup that always returns two results instead of one
A lookup that runs twice as fast as a normal one
questions.explain: A two-way lookup needs both a row condition and a column condition satisfied at once — a single lookup key isn't enough to identify the answer.

questions.q: In =INDEX(DataGrid, MATCH(region,RegionCol,0), MATCH(month,MonthRow,0)), what does the first MATCH find?
options: Which row region lives in
Which column month lives in
The total number of regions
Whether the grid has any errors
questions.explain: The first MATCH searches RegionCol and returns the row position for region; the second MATCH does the equivalent for month against MonthRow, giving INDEX both a row_num and col_num.

questions.q: Why does this two-way lookup work with two separate MATCH calls instead of one?
options: Each MATCH is independent — one finds a row position, the other a column position — and INDEX combines both coordinates to return the single intersecting cell
MATCH can only be used once per worksheet
One MATCH call always searches the entire workbook automatically
Two MATCH calls are required only for compatibility with older Excel versions
questions.explain: The two MATCH calls solve two separate axes of the same problem — row and column — which is exactly what INDEX's two-position form needs to isolate one cell.

questions.q: How does the nested XLOOKUP version of a two-way lookup work?
options: The inner XLOOKUP returns the entire matching row as an array, and the outer XLOOKUP searches within that row for the column value
XLOOKUP has a dedicated two-way lookup mode that requires no nesting
It requires converting the data to a PivotTable first
Nested XLOOKUP is not possible in any version of Excel
questions.explain: The inner XLOOKUP(region, RegionCol, DataGrid) returns the whole row for that region; the outer XLOOKUP then finds the month's position within just that row.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does INDEX/MATCH remain the more common choice for two-way lookups, even in workbooks that use XLOOKUP elsewhere?
options: It reads more symmetrically for two conditions than a nested XLOOKUP does
XLOOKUP cannot be nested under any circumstances
INDEX/MATCH is required by Excel for any grid with more than 10 rows
Nested XLOOKUP always produces incorrect results
questions.explain: The two independent MATCH calls inside one INDEX read more clearly for a genuinely two-dimensional problem than one XLOOKUP nested inside another.
